Executive Overview

This report analyzes 12,343 data points spanning 2015–2035 across six major economies to examine how AI automation is reshaping the global workforce. The findings reveal accelerating automation risk, widening compensation gaps, and clear skill-based survival patterns that demand immediate strategic attention.

  • Automation risk is accelerating. The average AI risk score climbs from 0.295 in 2015 to 0.508 by 2035—a 72% increase. The sharpest acceleration occurs post-2028, with risk rising 26.9% between 2024 and 2035 alone. Roles rooted in pattern recognition and structured data face the steepest trajectories.
  • Compensation and automation risk are inversely correlated. Higher-salary roles consistently exhibit lower AI risk scores (correlation: -0.245). Low-risk roles such as AI Researcher and Cybersecurity Analyst command median salaries 57% above high-risk roles like Business Analyst and Data Analyst.
  • Job survival prospects are deteriorating. The share of roles classified as "at risk" (survival class 0) grows from 8.9% in 2015 to 16.3% in 2035. Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles show the weakest survival outlook, with mean survival classes below 0.65.
  • Skills, not just titles, determine resilience. Deep Learning and Python-associated roles demonstrate the strongest survival profiles (mean survival class 1.58+), while Excel and SQL-centric roles cluster in the highest-risk tier. Java demand grows fastest (+5.1%), but Deep Learning maintains the highest survival premium.
  • Geographic divergence is modest but meaningful. India shows the highest average AI risk (0.401), while the USA offers the highest median compensation ($43,422) alongside strong survival rates. Cross-country salary gaps remain substantial even when normalized to USD.
Scope & Methodology Note

Data covers 10 job titles, 9 primary skills, 3 experience levels, and 3 education tiers across USA, UK, Germany, Canada, Australia, and India. Years 2015–2024 represent simulated historical baselines; 2025–2035 are forward projections based on trend extrapolation. All figures are derived directly from the dataset—no external estimates or fabricated values are used.

AI Automation Risk Landscape

Understanding which roles, regions, and experience profiles face the greatest automation exposure is the foundation of workforce planning. This section dissects the distribution and trajectory of AI risk scores across all key dimensions.

Risk Trajectory: The 2015–2035 Arc

The global average AI risk score follows a clear upward curve. From a baseline of 0.295 in 2015, risk escalates steadily through the early 2020s and accelerates post-2028, reaching 0.508 by 2035. This trajectory implies that roughly half of all tracked roles will face medium-to-high automation exposure by the end of the forecast period.

Figure 1: Average AI risk score rises from 0.295 (2015) to 0.508 (2035), with projection period beginning after 2024.

Risk by Job Role

Automation risk is not evenly distributed. Business Analyst roles carry the highest average risk score (0.750), followed by Data Analyst (0.649) and Software Engineer (0.447). At the opposite end, AI Researcher (0.150), Cybersecurity Analyst (0.251), and ML Engineer (0.253) demonstrate the strongest resilience.

Figure 2: Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles sit in the high-risk zone, while AI Researcher and Cybersecurity Analyst remain firmly in low-risk territory.

Risk by Geography

Country-level differences in AI risk are relatively narrow (range: 0.393–0.401), but directional signals matter. India records the highest average risk (0.401), potentially reflecting a higher concentration of routine-process roles in the dataset. The UK shows the lowest average risk (0.393). These differences should be interpreted with awareness of sample composition rather than as definitive national rankings.

Risk by Experience Level

Experience provides a meaningful buffer. Senior-level roles show lower average AI risk than Entry-level positions across nearly all job families. This pattern suggests that strategic judgment, stakeholder management, and complex decision-making—capabilities typically associated with seniority—are harder to automate than execution-oriented tasks.

Figure 3: Country bubble chart showing the interplay of automation risk, median compensation, and job survival rates. Bubble size corresponds to survival rate.

Key Risk Findings

  • The top three highest-risk roles (Business Analyst, Data Analyst, Software Engineer) account for a disproportionate share of total job openings—making their exposure a systemic concern.
  • Low-risk roles (AI Researcher, Cybersecurity Analyst, ML Engineer) are concentrated in specialized technical domains requiring deep expertise and contextual judgment.
  • Risk acceleration is sharpest in the 2028–2035 window, suggesting that near-term workforce planning must account for rapidly shifting automation boundaries.

Salary Trends & Segmentation

Compensation dynamics reveal both the premium commanded by resilient roles and the structural shifts unfolding across geographies and career stages. This section examines salary evolution and its explicit relationship with automation risk.

Global Salary Evolution

Median salaries rise from $24,247 in 2015 to $36,763 in 2035—a 52% nominal increase. However, growth is uneven: the USA maintains a persistent premium (median $43,422), while India remains at the lower end (median $12,448). All countries show positive nominal trajectories, but the absolute gaps widen in dollar terms.

Figure 4: Median salary trajectories by country. The USA maintains the highest compensation level throughout the forecast period.

Salary × Automation Risk Correlation

The dataset reveals a negative correlation of -0.245 between salary and AI risk score—higher compensation is systematically associated with lower automation exposure. This relationship is not coincidental: roles requiring creative problem-solving, security expertise, and advanced research command both higher pay and greater resilience.

Figure 5: Scatter plot of salary versus AI risk score, colored by job survival class. The downward trend line confirms the negative correlation (r = -0.245).

The compensation gap between risk tiers is stark. Median salaries by AI risk category:

  • Low Risk: $34,105
  • Medium Risk: $34,710
  • High Risk: $21,683

Low-risk roles pay 57% more than high-risk roles on average—a differential that has widened over time as automation compresses demand for routine analytical work.

Salary by Experience & Risk Category

Senior experience confers a substantial salary premium: Senior roles median at $48,318 versus $22,924 for Entry-level—a 111% gap. Critically, this premium is most pronounced in low-risk categories, suggesting that senior professionals in resilient fields capture compounding returns from both experience and role scarcity.

Figure 6: Median salary by experience level and AI risk category. Senior professionals in low-risk roles command the highest compensation.

Salary by Job Title

AI Researcher leads median compensation ($42,845), followed by ML Engineer ($39,327) and Product Manager ($37,947). Data Analyst ($18,692) and Business Analyst ($23,082) sit at the bottom—roles that also face the highest automation risk.

Compensation Insights

  • The salary–risk inverse relationship strengthens over time: by 2035, the gap between low-risk and high-risk median salaries exceeds $12,422.
  • Education level shows minimal direct salary impact in this dataset (Bachelor, Master, and PhD medians are within 2% of each other), suggesting that field of work and experience dominate compensation.
  • Geographic salary dispersion remains the single largest driver of absolute pay differences, with USA medians roughly 3.5× higher than India medians.

Skills Demand & Future-Proofing

Skills are the atomic unit of workforce resilience. This section identifies which competencies are gaining market relevance, how skill demand relates to survival outcomes, and which skill–role combinations offer the strongest protection against automation.

Skill Demand Trajectories

Average skill demand scores remain relatively stable across the forecast period (range: 78–81), but relative shifts tell a more important story. Java shows the fastest demand growth (+5.1% from 2015 to 2035), followed by Python (+3.7%) and AWS (+3.5%). Conversely, Docker demand contracts by 3.2% over the same period.

Figure 7: Skill demand score trajectories by primary skill. Java and Python show the strongest relative growth through 2035.

Skill Demand vs. Survival & Risk

Skill demand alone is not a perfect proxy for resilience. While Java demand grows fastest, roles centered on Deep Learning and Python achieve the highest mean survival classes (1.89 and 1.58, respectively). This divergence indicates that what the skill enables matters as much as how much it is demanded.

Highest-Resilience Skill–Role Combination

The strongest survival profile in the dataset is AI Researcher with Deep Learning (mean survival class: 1.89). This combination pairs cutting-edge technical depth with a role that inherently requires creative and strategic judgment.

Strategic Skill Insights

  • Deep Learning is the single strongest predictor of job survival (mean class 1.89), despite modest demand growth. Organizations should treat Deep Learning expertise as a scarcity asset.
  • Excel and SQL are associated with the weakest survival profiles (0.43 and 0.56, respectively). These skills are not disappearing, but their value is commoditizing as AI automates routine data manipulation.
  • Python offers the best balance of high demand, strong survival, and broad applicability across Data Science, ML Engineering, and AI Research roles.
  • Security skills maintain a stable demand profile with low AI risk (0.25) and strong survival (1.53)—a defensive pillar for any workforce portfolio.

Job Survival & Market Outlook

Job survival class distributions and opening trends reveal which combinations of role, skill, education, and geography yield the strongest prospects through 2035—and where the workforce is most vulnerable.

Survival Rate Trajectory

The proportion of roles classified as surviving (class ≥ 1) declines from 91.1% in 2015 to 83.7% in 2035. This 7.4 percentage-point erosion is driven primarily by the reclassification of Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles from moderate to at-risk status as AI capabilities advance.

Figure 8: Stacked area chart showing the evolving distribution of job survival classes. The at-risk segment (red) expands most sharply after 2028.

Job Openings: Volume vs. Resilience

Total job openings show modest growth (+5.8% from 2015 to 2035), peaking around 2019 at 15.9 million openings. However, volume masks vulnerability: the roles with the highest opening counts (Business Analyst, Data Analyst, Software Engineer) are also among the most automation-exposed.

Figure 9: Total job openings by role over time. High-volume roles do not necessarily equate to high-resilience roles.

Survival by Role, Education & Experience

The heatmap below distills survival strength across the role–education matrix. AI Researcher and ML Engineer roles show strong survival (1.7+) regardless of education level, while Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles remain below 1.0 across all education tiers. Education provides a modest boost within roles but cannot fully compensate for role-level risk exposure.

Figure 10: Mean job survival class by role and education level. Darker green indicates stronger survival prospects.

Experience level reinforces survival outcomes. Senior professionals average a survival class of 1.57, compared to 1.06 for Entry-level—a gap of 0.51 points. This pattern holds across all major role categories and underscores the protective value of seniority.

Survival Outlook Summary

  • Strongest prospects: AI Researcher, ML Engineer, Cybersecurity Analyst—regardless of geography or education, these roles maintain survival classes above 1.5.
  • Weakest prospects: Business Analyst (0.43) and Data Analyst (0.56) show consistently poor survival, with limited differentiation by education or experience.
  • Moderate prospects: Software Engineer (1.18), Product Manager (1.44), Cloud Engineer (1.48), Data Scientist (1.44), and DevOps Engineer (1.56) occupy a middle tier where experience and specialization can tip outcomes.
  • Geographic factor: Country effects on survival are secondary to role and skill effects. The right role in India outperforms the wrong role in the USA.

Strategic Recommendations

The following recommendations are grounded directly in the dataset findings. Each traces to a specific quantitative insight and is designed for executive decision-making on talent investment, reskilling, and workforce planning.

1. Prioritize Reskilling Away from High-Risk Skill Stacks

Data Foundation

Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles face AI risk scores of 0.750 and 0.649, with mean survival classes of 0.43 and 0.56 respectively. Excel and SQL skills show the weakest survival association (0.43 and 0.56).

Action: Redirect reskilling investment from Excel/SQL-heavy analytical tracks toward Python, Deep Learning, and Security skill stacks. Target the 11.0% of the workforce currently in at-risk classifications for priority upskilling. Partner with technical universities and online platforms to accelerate credentialing in these domains.

2. Defend and Expand Low-Risk Technical Roles

Data Foundation

AI Researcher, Cybersecurity Analyst, and ML Engineer roles combine low AI risk (≤0.25) with high median salaries ($42,845, $27,658, $39,327) and strong survival (≥1.53).

Action: Increase headcount targets and compensation bands for AI Research, Cybersecurity, and ML Engineering by 20–30% above current plans. These roles are scarcity assets: their low risk and high pay signal a supply–demand imbalance that will intensify through 2035. Establish dedicated recruitment pipelines and retention bonuses.

3. Leverage the Experience Premium

Data Foundation

Senior-level professionals show a 111% salary premium and a 0.51-point survival class advantage over Entry-level peers. This protective effect is consistent across all job families.

Action: Accelerate leadership and strategic-judgment development programs for Mid-level talent. The data suggests that experience-based capabilities (stakeholder management, architecture decisions, creative problem-solving) are harder to automate and more valuable than incremental technical training alone. Fast-track high-potential Mid-level employees into Senior roles before 2028, when risk acceleration steepens.

4. Diversify Geographic Talent Strategy

Data Foundation

The USA commands a 249% salary premium over India, but role-level survival effects dominate country effects. India shows the highest average AI risk (0.401) among tracked countries.

Action: Build resilient teams by prioritizing role mix over location arbitrage. Offshoring high-risk roles (e.g., routine data analysis) to lower-cost markets amplifies systemic vulnerability. Instead, distribute low-risk roles (AI Research, Security) across geographies to capture cost advantages without compounding automation exposure. In high-risk countries like India, aggressively upskill local workforces toward Python, Security, and Deep Learning.

5. Monitor the 2028 Inflection Point

Data Foundation

AI risk acceleration is sharpest post-2028, with the average risk score climbing from 0.400 (2024) to 0.508 (2035)—a 26.9% increase in just 11 years. Job survival rates drop from ~86% (2024) to 83.7% (2035).

Action: Treat 2028 as a strategic checkpoint. By 2027, complete workforce risk audits, finalize reskilling cohorts, and renegotiate role mixes with outsourcing partners. The post-2028 period will reward organizations that have already shifted their talent portfolios toward low-risk, high-skill configurations.

6. Invest in Python as a Universal Workforce Language

Data Foundation

Python is the most versatile skill in the dataset: it underpins Data Scientist, ML Engineer, and AI Researcher roles (all survival class ≥1.44), shows strong demand growth (+3.7%), and carries a low-to-moderate AI risk profile.

Action: Mandate Python proficiency as a baseline requirement for all technical and analytical hires by 2027. Launch internal Python academies for existing staff in moderate-risk roles (Software Engineer, Cloud Engineer, DevOps Engineer) to expand their mobility into higher-resilience positions.
